The chairperson of FIDA, Chioma Onyenucheya-Uko, highlighted the challenges during an interview on Leadership TV, hosted by Grace Ike, while discussing the sexual assault allegation involving the Emir of Daura and the response of the Katsina State Government.
She said many survivors remain silent or abandon attempts to seek justice because they fear disbelief, public humiliation and possible rejection by their communities or workplaces.
According to her, the situation becomes more complicated when allegations involve individuals in positions of authority, as complainants may feel intimidated or fear retaliation.
On the issue of consent, Onyenucheya-Uko stressed that a woman’s decision to visit a man, sit close to him or agree to a particular form of physical contact should not be interpreted as blanket consent to further sexual activity.
She explained that consent must be voluntary and specific and could be withdrawn at any point.
However, she cautioned against reaching conclusions on the Daura allegation before the investigation is concluded, emphasising that the accused is also entitled to due process and the presumption of innocence.
Assessing Katsina State’s response, she described the reported suspension of the Emir’s official engagements and the constitution of an investigative committee as steps in the right direction.
She, however, stressed that the investigation must produce a clear outcome and that any evidence of criminal conduct should be referred to the appropriate law enforcement authorities.
The FIDA chairperson identified weaknesses in evidence collection, preservation and presentation as factors that could undermine the prosecution of sexual violence cases.
She said unsuccessful prosecutions should not be blamed solely on the courts, noting that shortcomings in police investigations and prosecution processes could also affect the outcome of cases.
Onyenucheya-Uko also called for procedures that reduce the burden on survivors, particularly repeated interviews and the distress of recounting traumatic experiences to different authorities.
On the legal and institutional response, she highlighted measures introduced in Katsina State to address gender-based violence, including the domestication of the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) law, establishment of a specialised court and a Sexual Assault Referral Centre.
She said the structures would only make a meaningful difference if they were adequately implemented, supported by trained personnel and made accessible to people seeking justice.
The FIDA chairperson further noted that sexual violence affects people beyond women and girls, stressing that boys, men, children, persons with disabilities and older people could also be vulnerable.
She emphasised the need to recognise male survivors, particularly boys who may struggle to report abuse because of shame, fear or societal expectations.
Onyenucheya-Uko said the broader challenge was to ensure that the justice system protected complainants without denying accused persons a fair hearing.
She added that public confidence in the justice system depended on its ability to investigate allegations properly, protect those who report abuse and determine cases based on credible evidence.
